Evidence for Impact.

Solutions that Last.

Resustainovation Lab is an emerging research and innovation lab built on a simple hypothesis: development work becomes more effective when locally generated evidence, sustainability thinking, and practical innovation are treated as one connected process — not three separate ones.

The problem we are testing

Decisions are often made faster than evidence can be produced.

In many recovery and development settings, programmes are designed under time pressure, with limited local data, and evaluated after the fact. Useful knowledge does exist — but it is scattered across reports, hard to compare, rarely local enough to guide a specific district, and almost never handed back to the communities that produced it.

We are not claiming to have solved this. We are stating it as the problem worth working on, and proposing a way to test whether a small, locally embedded lab can close part of the gap.

Gap 01

Evidence arrives late

Findings are frequently published after the decision window has already closed.

Gap 02

Data is not local enough

National averages hide district-level realities that determine whether an intervention works.

Gap 03

Knowledge does not return home

Communities contribute data but rarely receive it back in a usable, open form.

Gap 04

Innovation stays theoretical

Good ideas are seldom prototyped, tested, and documented in the field where they must work.

How we work

A four-step pathway, designed to be repeatable

Each step produces something the next step can use. The point is not a single study — it is a loop that keeps improving decisions.

01

Research

Start from questions that practitioners and residents actually need answered, using methods proportionate to the decision at hand.

02

Evidence

Turn findings into structured, comparable, openly accessible outputs — briefs, datasets, and plain-language summaries.

03

Innovation

Prototype practical responses with the people who will use them, then test them at small scale before recommending anything.

04

Sustainable Impact

Hand over tools, skills, and data locally, so results outlive the project cycle that funded them.

Research

Questions first, methods second

The research function is intended to be small, focused, and useful. Rather than pursuing broad academic agendas, it starts with decisions someone is about to make and asks what evidence would change them.

Each study is scoped around a specific decision — a service design choice, a targeting question, a delivery bottleneck — with an agreed deadline set by that decision, not by publication cycles.
Household and facility surveys, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, secondary data review, and light-touch monitoring — combined at whatever depth the question genuinely requires.
Data is planned to be collected by trained local enumerators, with community consultation built into design and interpretation rather than added at the end.
Informed consent, data minimisation, secure storage, and do-no-harm review are treated as preconditions for fieldwork. Sensitive data will not be published in identifiable form.
Anonymised data, instruments, and methods notes are intended for open publication so others can reuse, challenge, or replicate the work.
Innovation

Prototypes, not proposals

Evidence only matters if something changes because of it. The innovation function is designed to translate findings into things people can actually try — and to be honest when a prototype does not work.

◆

Co-design with users

Solutions are shaped with the residents, practitioners, and local authorities who would operate them, from the first sketch onward.

▲

Small-scale testing

Test at the smallest scale that can still produce a credible answer, then decide whether to iterate, stop, or expand.

●

Low-cost and repairable

Preference for approaches that can be maintained locally with available materials, skills, and budgets.

■

Documented openly

Build notes, costs, and failure points are written down so others do not have to repeat the same learning curve.

◇

Sustainability screened

Environmental footprint, running cost, and ownership after handover are assessed before anything is recommended.

△

Fail-forward culture

Negative results are published as findings. A prototype that fails cheaply and early is a useful outcome.

Flagship pilot · Proof of concept

The Salamiyah District Pilot

A 12-month, deliberately small proof of concept in Salamiyah District, Syria, with an indicative budget of USD 40,000. Its purpose is to test whether the lab model works in practice before anyone considers scaling it.

Salamiyah District offers a realistic but manageable setting: a defined geography where recovery, service delivery, and livelihood questions overlap, and where a small team can work closely with local actors rather than at a distance.

Choosing one district is a deliberate constraint. It keeps the pilot affordable, makes accountability concrete, and means the lab is judged on whether it was actually useful to a specific place — not on how many locations it appeared in.

12-month durationUSD 40,000 indicativeSingle district
Hypothesis 1

Can useful local evidence be produced quickly and cheaply?

Test whether a small team can deliver decision-ready studies within timeframes and budgets that local actors can realistically sustain.

Hypothesis 2

Will anyone actually use it?

Track whether published evidence is accessed, cited, or referenced in real planning and programme decisions.

Hypothesis 3

Can prototypes move from idea to field test?

Check whether co-designed responses reach a testable state and produce clear keep, adapt, or drop decisions.

Hypothesis 4

Does local capacity remain afterwards?

Assess whether trained local researchers, tools, and datasets stay available and in use beyond the pilot period.

Months 1–2 · Set-up

Register activities and permissions, recruit a small core team, establish ethics and data protection protocols, and confirm partnerships with local actors.

Months 2–4 · Needs and question setting

Consult communities, service providers, and authorities to agree the priority questions the pilot will answer.

Months 4–7 · First research cycle

Train local enumerators, collect and analyse data, and produce the first evidence briefs and anonymised datasets.

Months 6–9 · Co-design and prototyping

Translate findings into one or more practical prototypes with the people who would use them, and begin small-scale testing.

Months 9–11 · Publish and convene

Release outputs through the Evidence Portal, hold local feedback sessions, and document what worked and what did not.

Month 12 · Independent review

Evaluate the pilot against its own targets and publish an honest assessment, including a recommendation on whether to continue, adjust, or stop.

Indicative allocation — USD 40,000

Illustrative planning split for a lean 12-month pilot. Final figures depend on funding agreements and local costs.

Governance and accountability

Activities are planned to run through formal agreements with local organisations and relevant authorities, defining roles, data ownership, and community consent.
An advisory group of researchers and practitioners is intended to review study design and interpretation, providing independent challenge.
Progress against targets, spending categories, and lessons learned are intended for public reporting — including where targets are missed.

Stakeholder ecosystem

Who this only works with

A lab this size cannot function alone. Each group below brings something the model depends on — and gets something specific back.

⌂
Communities

Set priorities, take part in design, and receive findings back in plain language.

⚑
Local authorities

Provide access and context; gain district-level evidence for planning decisions.

◎
NGOs & agencies

Bring operational questions; use shared evidence to avoid duplicated assessments.

⚛
Universities

Contribute methods rigour and review; gain field-grounded research opportunities.

◈
Funders

Enable the pilot; receive transparent reporting, including negative results.

Principles

The commitments we want to be held to

Locally led

Local researchers, local questions, local ownership of data and tools.

Evidence before advocacy

We describe what we find, including when it is inconvenient or inconclusive.

Open by default

Methods, instruments, and anonymised data are published for reuse and scrutiny.

Do no harm

Consent, privacy, and safeguarding come before any research or publication objective.

Sustainability as a test

If a solution cannot be maintained locally, we do not count it as a success.

Honest about uncertainty

We label what is a hypothesis, what is a target, and what has actually been measured.

About the lab

An emerging lab, described honestly

Resustainovation Lab is at an early stage. There is a model, a pilot plan, and a clear set of principles — and there is not yet a portfolio of completed studies. This website describes intent and design, not a track record.

The name joins three ideas the lab refuses to separate: research, sustainability, and innovation. The emblem expresses the same thing — a triangle held together by a network of connected nodes, because none of the three points stands up on its own.

Stage: pilot in designNo completed studies yet
Founder

Enas Fatoom

Founder, Resustainovation Lab

The lab was founded by Enas Fatoom, whose background spans international development, project management, public health, sustainability, research, and community engagement.

That combination is the reason the lab is structured the way it is: evidence, delivery, and community participation treated as parts of the same job rather than separate departments.

The Spark
“The idea did not begin with a strategy document. It began with a decision to stop waiting for someone else to produce the evidence.”

Resustainovation Lab was conceived on 13 December 2025 — the moment the idea was written down and given a name. It is recorded here not as an achievement, but as a starting point: everything on this site follows from that decision, and remains to be tested.
